meta.title: How designers actually work with AI
meta.note: Ten designers at nine companies. Every tool, handoff and reason is quoted from a full interview, timestamped to the moment it was said.

axis.grounding: Five phases every one of the six moves through. Danny and Kazden both describe the explore-to-refine spine themselves, Danny at 10:52, Kazden at 10:42. Movement runs both ways.

stages.label: Gather
stages.blurb: Signal in, inspiration, customer voice, what was actually said in the room

stages.label: Frame
stages.blurb: Turn raw signal into something you can act on

stages.label: Explore
stages.blurb: Go wide and rough, many directions, nothing precious

stages.label: Build
stages.blurb: Make it real in code, against the real design system

stages.label: Ship
stages.blurb: Out to engineers, stakeholders and production

designers.name: Danny Williams
designers.thesis: Tools sit on a spectrum. One end is exploring: messy, generative, wide. The other is refining: precise, deliberate, narrow.

source.title: AI Native Workflow of a Designer at Wealthsimple

designers.name: Kazden Cattapan
designers.thesis: Claude Code is all you need. The terminal is just the interface. The markdown skill files are the magic.

source.title: How I use Claude Code as a Designer at Shopify

designers.name: Clint McManaman
designers.thesis: Go friction hunting every week. Do not wait for a PRD. Read the feedback yourself and bring the experiment.

source.title: AI Native Designer shows his Growth Design Process

designers.name: John Voss
designers.thesis: Automate the background context building, then carry anything AI touched over the finish line yourself.

source.title: How Notion + Claude makes me a 2x Design Manager

designers.name: Claire Taylor
designers.thesis: Scrappy on purpose. Barely a design system, one page of pointers to the engineer, then polish it in code yourself.

source.title: Designer at Early Stage Startup Shows Her Workflow

designers.name: Jennifer Spriggs
designers.thesis: Learn Git. Branches are how you hold variants, and one link with a switcher beats four links.

designers.name: Andy McClelland
designers.thesis: Discovery first. Speeding up in the wrong direction is still a waste.

source.title: How I do AI Prototyping as a Designer in Healthcare

designers.name: Karl Koch
designers.thesis: A deliberately tiny stack. Figma is a scratchpad, and 80 percent of the work happens in Cursor.

source.title: Design Engineer at DuckDuckGo Shows His Workflow

designers.name: Christina Kim
designers.thesis: Pick the tool by what you need to learn: speed, polish, or design system accuracy.

source.title: How I Vibe Code as a Designer using AI Tools at Descript

designers.name: Henry Modisett
designers.thesis: Write the document first. Visuals too early become a rabbit hole before the mechanics are settled.

source.title: Why Designers at Perplexity skip Figma to design directly in code

choices.criterion: Is this something I'm going to refine, or something I'm going to invent? Refining a real flow goes to Magic Patterns, because the design system is wired in. Inventing something that doesn't exist yet goes to Claude, free of those constraints.
Going wide and the precise details don't matter yet, Claude Design. Dialling in details, or actually shipping, Conductor or Claude Code.
Worktrees in the terminal are cumbersome. A well-designed GUI beats a terminal any day.
Everything in Paper is already HTML and CSS so Claude builds from it far more accurately, nothing has to translate.
The intelligence plus MCP plus markdown skills is the unlock. The terminal is just the interface and Cursor's chat feels clunkier.
AI-first experiences are very hard to do statically in Figma, because the possibilities of a conversation are open-ended.
Fluid drag-and-drop was hours of stop-motion frames in Figma and minutes in code and it tests far better.
Branches hold variants properly, so one link with a switcher replaces a pile of separate prototypes.
Ask mode more than anything else, highlight something, ask what it does, learn the codebase without breaking it.
Claude summarising a board beat Figma's native export, you get a true summary, not the raw data in a readable format.
AI prototyping is a game changer, but speeding up in the wrong direction is still a waste. Discovery settles the direction first.
Developing a flat idea then putting it into code meant too much back and forth. Now the idea goes straight into code.
If a simple interaction can be stitched from mocks you already have, a plain Figma prototype gets the job done.
Figma Make and Cursor already carry the design system. Replit is for starting from scratch, when nothing has to match.
Does it need real data to show how it works? Then Cursor. If it reads in isolation, Figma Make.
Visuals too early are a rabbit hole. A written document formulates the vision before anything is drawn.
